title: PID control
ends: Your loops will run on auto.

steps.q: A P-only level loop settles a little below set point. What removes that offset?
steps.title: Offset
steps.summary: A proportional-only controller changes output in proportion to error, so after a load change it needs a standing error to hold the new valve position, and the process settles off set point. Integral action adds up the error over time and keeps moving the output until the error is zero. Most process loops are PI.

draw: integral: adds up error until it's zero

steps.q: You keep raising the controller gain to make a loop faster. What happens in the end?
steps.title: Too much gain
steps.summary: Raising controller gain makes a loop respond faster, but past a point it overreacts and oscillates around set point, and can become unstable. Low gain is slow; good gain gives a quick response with a small, settling overshoot. If a loop cycles, put it in manual: if the cycling stops, look at tuning or a sticking valve; if it continues, the disturbance is coming from upstream.

steps.q: Why do most flow loops run without derivative action?
board: Why do most flow loops run
steps.title: Noise
steps.summary: Flow measurements are noisy, and derivative action responds to the rate of change, so each jitter produces a large output kick. The valve then twitches constantly, wearing it out and making control worse. Flow and pressure loops are usually PI; derivative is mainly useful on slow loops with clean signals, such as some temperature loops.

opts.t: Flow loops are too slow for it

steps.q: Cooling water valve on the jacket of an exothermic reactor. Which way should it fail on loss of air?
board: it fail on loss of air?
steps.title: Fail-safe
steps.summary: Choose each valve's failure position by asking what is safe if the air or signal is lost. On an exothermic reactor, losing cooling is the danger, so the jacket cooling water valve fails open. Steam or heating valves fail closed so heat stops, and dosing valves fail closed so addition stops. Confirm each fail position in the HAZOP, since overcooling can be a hazard on some batches.

steps.q: In a cascade for reactor temperature, which loop is the inner (slave) loop?
steps.title: Cascade
steps.summary: In a reactor temperature cascade, the outer (master) loop controls batch temperature and its output is the set point of the inner (slave) loop, which controls jacket temperature by moving the valve. The fast inner loop corrects upsets such as cooling water temperature changes before the batch feels them. Tune the inner loop first; it must be several times faster than the outer loop.

steps.q: A valve sits at 100 % for a long time, then the PV overshoots badly. What is this?
board: a long time, then the PV
steps.title: Windup
steps.summary: When a valve is saturated, for example fully open, and the process still cannot reach set point, integral action keeps accumulating error and the controller output winds up far beyond its limit. When the process variable finally reaches set point, the integral must unwind before the valve moves, so the process overshoots. Anti-windup clamps the integral at the output limit; check it is enabled.

intro.text: Hi, I'm Bubbles. Today: PID loops, the reason the operator isn't turning valves all day. Six questions. Ready?

outro-web.text: That's the lesson. Read the PID tuning guide next.

q1.text: Question 1. A P-only level loop settles a little below set point. What removes that offset?

q1-r0.text: Derivative reacts to change. A steady offset doesn't change.

q1-r1.text: Integral! It keeps pushing until the error is zero.

q1-r2.text: A bigger valve doesn't change the controller maths.

q1-r3.text: Lower gain makes the offset bigger, not smaller.

q1-b0.text: A proportional-only controller moves the valve in proportion to the error. No error, no extra output.

q1-b1.text: So after a load change it needs some error to hold the new valve position. It settles just off set point.

q1-b2.text: Integral adds up the error over time and keeps moving the valve until the error is gone.

q1-b3.text: That's why most process loops are PI: proportional for speed, integral to finish the job.

q2.text: Question 2. You keep raising the controller gain to make a loop faster. What happens in the end?

q2-r0.text: Forever? Every loop has a limit, and it isn't pretty.

q2-r1.text: Yes! Too much gain and it swings around the set point.

q2-r2.text: More gain shrinks the offset. Something else goes wrong.

q2-r3.text: The valve moves more, not less. That's the problem.

q2-b0.text: Low gain: slow and steady. It creeps up to set point.

q2-b1.text: Good gain: quick, with a small overshoot that settles.

q2-b2.text: Too much gain: the valve overreacts every time. The loop swings, and can keep swinging.

q2-b3.text: If a loop cycles, put it in manual. If the cycling stops, it's the tuning or a sticky valve. If it carries on, it's coming from upstream.

q3.text: Question 3. Why do most flow loops run without derivative action?

q3-r0.text: Slow? Flow loops are the fastest loops in the plant.

q3-r1.text: Correct! Noisy signal plus derivative equals a twitchy valve.

q3-r3.text: The DCS allows it. Good engineers don't.

q3-b0.text: Flow signals are noisy. The reading jitters even when the flow is steady.

q3-b1.text: Derivative acts on the rate of change. Each little jitter looks like a big, fast change.

q3-b2.text: So the valve twitches all day. It wears out, and the loop gets worse, not better.

q3-b3.text: Flow and pressure loops are usually PI. Derivative helps slow loops with a clean signal, like some temperature loops.

q4.text: Question 4. Cooling water valve on the jacket of an exothermic reactor. Which way should it fail on loss of air?

q4-r0.text: Fail closed? Lose air and you lose cooling, mid-reaction.

q4-r1.text: Fail open. Lose air, keep cooling. Correct!

q4-r2.text: Last position might be nearly shut. Not good enough here.

q4-r3.text: It matters a lot on an exothermic batch.

q4-b0.text: Ask one question: what's safe if the air supply or the signal is lost?

q4-b1.text: For an exothermic reactor, losing cooling is the danger. So the cooling water valve fails open.

q4-b2.text: A steam or heating valve fails closed. Losing air should stop the heat, not add more.

q4-b3.text: The same goes for the dosing valve. Lose air, stop dosing. Fail closed. Confirm every fail position in the HAZOP.

q5.text: Question 5. In a cascade for reactor temperature, which loop is the inner (slave) loop?

q5-r0.text: That's the master. It tells the inner loop what to do.

q5-r1.text: Yes! The jacket loop is inside, quick and close to the valve.

q5-r2.text: The agitator isn't part of this cascade.

q5-r3.text: Level doesn't come into reactor temperature control here.

q5-b0.text: The outer, master loop watches the batch temperature. It is slow, because the batch is big.

q5-b1.text: Its output isn't a valve position. It's a set point for the jacket temperature.

q5-b2.text: The inner, slave loop holds the jacket at that set point. It's fast, and fixes upsets like a change in water temperature before the batch feels them.

q5-b3.text: Tune the inner loop first, then the outer one. The inner loop must be several times faster.

q6.text: Question 6. A valve sits at 100 % for a long time, then the PV overshoots badly. What is this?

q6-r0.text: Stiction makes small jumps. This is a big, late overshoot.

q6-r1.text: Integral windup! The integral kept adding while the valve couldn't move.

q6-r2.text: Derivative doesn't store anything up. Something else does.

q6-r3.text: The transmitter read it right. The controller overdid it.

q6-b0.text: The valve is wide open but still can't reach set point. The error stays.

q6-b1.text: Integral keeps adding up that error. The controller output winds far beyond 100 percent, inside the maths.

q6-b2.text: When the PV finally gets there, the integral has to unwind first. The valve stays open too long, and the PV overshoots.

q6-b3.text: Anti-windup clamps the integral when the output hits its limit. Check it's switched on in your DCS. Read the PID tuning guide on pharmacheme dot in for more.
